change: on-disk graph adjacency tables (adj_out / adj_in multimaps in the .graph file): checked once per open, catch-up of edges an older binary added, chunked diff sync, key-sorted batch inserts
snapshot: benchmarks/dogfood-recall/data/snap-prefix (copy of this repo's .axil): 161,373 edges, .graph edges-only, 120,713,216 bytes

binaries.base: axil 2.3.1 built from dev 65d45ff (no adjacency tables; loads every edge into memory on first graph use)

method: Each case runs on its own APFS clone (cp -c -R) of the snapshot. size_bytes = st_size, the logical length that ls and `axil info` report. allocated_bytes = st_blocks * 512, the disk actually used (what du reports): redb grows a file by set_len, which leaves an unwritten, sparse tail. in_use_bytes = allocated_pages * page_size from redb 3.1.3 WriteTransaction::stats(), the pages holding data. cpu_s = user + sys seconds from /usr/bin/time -p for that one command. The machine had a 1-minute load average of 86-102 from other jobs during the runs, so cpu_s is indicative only and no wall time is recorded. The probe record for `edges` is entity 01KVCKTC05AJ45EYK82SFWRM6A; `link` goes between decisions 01KVCT6BGMW3HM1GF3JQHBXSR5 and 01KVEVDNRTAZW4NCMX1YHJRS5R.

first_graph_use.command: axil edges <entity> on the edges-only snapshot (the new binary builds the adjacency tables, 322,746 entries)

ingest_scip_on_migrated_copy.command: axil ingest-scip .axil/index-rust.scip; both binaries wrote 25,507 new edges and deduplicated 176,527
ingest_scip_on_migrated_copy.note: The new binary's one ingest transaction copies most pages of both adjacency tables. Once the free pages inside the file run out, redb doubles a file this size (single region) rather than growing it by what it needs, so the logical length went from 120.7 MB to 241.4 MB while the disk used grew by 23.4 MB. Sorting batch inserts by key does not change this: redb copies a page once per transaction and edits the copy in place after that, whatever the insert order.

ingest_scip_on_unmigrated_copy.command: same ingest with the new binary straight on the edges-only snapshot (build the tables, then ingest, in one process)

binary_switching.command: three rounds of: base binary `axil link`, then `axil edges <entity>` (new binary on the new copy, base binary on the base copy)
binary_switching.note: The new binary catches up by reading only the edges after the stamped greatest id.

older_binary_delete_then_read.command: base binary `axil delete` of the linked decision (removes its edges), then `axil edges <entity>`; the new binary has to diff every edge

redb_compact_on_copies.method: Each file comes from re-running the matching case above on a fresh clone (same lengths; disk use within 33 KB of the case's). A standalone probe linked against redb 3.1.3, the version this workspace locks, opens a clone of the file, reads stats(), runs Database::compact() once (it loops internally until no page moves) and drops the handle. after_close is read after the drop, because redb's closing commit changes the file. seconds = wall time of open + stats + compact at a load average of about 50. snapshot = the base binary's file (its first use writes nothing); new_migrated = first_graph_use new; new_after_ingest and base_after_ingest = ingest_scip_on_migrated_copy new and base.
redb_compact_on_copies.reopen_cycles: Three more open/close cycles of each compacted file kept its length and grew its disk use by at most 48 KiB: a doubled length stays.
redb_compact_on_copies.variation: The adversarial review compacted its own clone of new_after_ingest with its own probe and got 139,595,776 bytes long and allocated: that close fit without growing. Both probes run here got 279,060,480 on this clone. Whether a close doubles a packed file can't be told in advance.
redb_compact_on_copies.why_the_length_doubles: redb writes its allocator state on every close (the quick-repair commit in Database::drop), which needs new pages. compact() leaves none free (ShrinkPolicy::Maximum), and redb grows a file smaller than one region (4 GiB at 4 KiB pages) to twice its size. The added half is never written, so it costs length, and disk only on a filesystem without holes. A quick-repair commit of our own before the drop grew the compacted snapshot the same way, from 70,463,488 to 140,922,880 bytes long.
redb_compact_on_copies.killed_midway: A kill 6 s into compacting a clone of new_after_ingest left it 139,563,008 bytes long; the next `axil edges <entity>` (0.47 s wall) printed the same as on the uncompacted file.
redb_compact_on_copies.conclusion: compact() lowered disk use in every case: by 50.2 MB (41.6%) on snapshot, 1.5 MB (1.3%) on new_migrated, 4.4 MB (3.1%) on new_after_ingest and 40.1 MB (33.2%) on base_after_ingest. The close after it doubled the length in 3 of 4 cases (+16.7%, +97.4%, +15.6%). The files the new binary writes hold data in 96.9-98.7% of their disk use, so compacting them gives back little and can double what ls shows and what a copy that doesn't keep holes writes. So `axil compact` compacts the .graph file only when at most 40% of its disk use holds data (axil_graph::compact_graph_store). Below 50% the doubled result is no larger than before by length or disk use on any filesystem; the margin keeps a file just compacted on a filesystem without holes, then about half data, from being compacted on every run. None of these four files passes; a store after many edges are deleted does (tests compacting_a_store_with_most_edges_deleted_gives_back_disk in axil-graph and compact_gives_back_the_pages_of_deleted_edges in axil-cli).

axil_compact_on_copies.method: This branch's release build ran `axil compact` on clones of the new_migrated and new_after_ingest database directories above. seconds = wall time of the whole command at a load average of about 60, of which db.compact() (record purge and orphan cleanup, unchanged by this branch) took 12.7 s and 13.4 s.
